title: Lakehaven - token velocity and deploy mode eval
summary: Intro + discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming and burst throughput. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private due to compliance and real-time SLAs. Agreed to run a 48-hour benchmark with sample traffic. Next: pricing spreadsheet, SOC2 docs, benchmark coordination.
next_steps: Marcus to schedule 48-hour benchmark and share test harness (due 2026-07-23)
Priya to send hosted/dedicated/private pricing matrix and SOC2 + architecture diagram (due 2026-07-20)
Tom to upload sample prompts, traffic histogram and representative payloads (due 2026-07-21)
action_items: Marcus Lee: setup benchmark run and provide test script (due 2026-07-23)
Priya Nair: send pricing spreadsheet and SOC2 deck (due 2026-07-20)
Tom Rivers: provide sample prompts and traffic profile (due 2026-07-21)
transcript:
[00:00] Priya Nair: hi everyone uh i'm priya with Redwood, thanks for joining. we have marcus from engineering. how's lakehaven doing today?
[00:04] Sofia Delgado: good thanks. yes, a few of us joining, i'm sofia, cto. tom's here, aisha's here for security.
[00:09] Tom Rivers: hey, morning all. quick agenda — latency/throughput constraints, our current infra, talk hosting options, then decide bench next steps.
[00:16] Marcus Lee: quick note — i'll run through our benchmark plan later and then coordinate the run.
[00:20] Sofia Delgado: perfect. quick background — we run a live transcription + docs summarization product for maritime operations. typical interactions are short queries, 40-200 tokens responses, but we also have streaming transcripts where tokens arrive continuously. our SLA is pretty strict: p95 end-to-end generation for small replies needs to be under 300-350ms, and streaming per-token latency ideally < 50ms p95 at steady state.
[00:44] Priya Nair: thanks that's really helpful. when you say end-to-end, are you including network hop from client to model in that p95, or just inference engine time?
[00:52] Sofia Delgado: total from request to first token display — so network + processing. most of our users are on mobile with variable LTE. we accept a little network variability but want the inference portion to be as predictable as possible.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: noted. so for hosted vs dedicated vs private, the big differences for your case will be: predictable warm capacity and routing locality. dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and less noisy neighbor impact; private (VPC/on-prem) addresses egress and data residency but adds ops overhead. hosted is fastest to get started but you hit multi-tenant noise.
[01:30] Tom Rivers: can you quantify the p95 numbers we should expect for a model like Llama-variant 7B or similar when optimized? we're evaluating quantized variants too.
[01:40] Marcus Lee: rough ballpark: for a 7B optimized and running on a modern A100 equivalent, single-stream generation to produce 100 tokens might be in the 120-250ms range inference-only, depending on batching and kv-cache. per-token streaming after prefix is usually < 20-40ms p95 if we keep the request pinned and KV cache warm. with quantization you trade some accuracy but can shave cycles — int8-like runs can be 1.3–1.6x faster but depends on kernel paths.
[02:12] Aisha Khan: and reliability for us is huge — audit logs, KMS integration, SOC2. if we went hosted, can we still do customer-managed keys?
[02:21] Priya Nair: yes, hosted supports external KMS for enterprise tiers; we can integrate with AWS KMS or partner HSMs. audit logs and token-level tracing are available in the console. for the strictest compliance you'd look at Private — full control plane in your VPC.
[02:38] Sofia Delgado: okay. traffic profile: bursty — during docking windows we get spikes up to 1200 concurrent streams for ~5-10 minute windows. steady-state is more like 60-120 concurrent. bursts are main concern.
[02:54] Marcus Lee: good detail. our Dedicated product supports burst capacity and autoscaling with pre-warmed pools — you can configure a reserved baseline and a short-term burst headroom. also fallback policies allow routing to cheaper model variants if primary capacity is saturated.
[03:11] Tom Rivers: what's the cold-start behaviour? when a new container spins up, how long until the model warms?
[03:17] Marcus Lee: cold-start typically depends on model size and quantization — for a 7B it might be 10-30s to load weights if not cached; we mitigate with continuous batching and optional keepalive pre-warms for critical routes. for streaming customers we recommend a small pool always warm for p95 guarantees.
[03:34] Sofia Delgado: ok, we're leaning toward either Dedicated or Private. key questions: cost delta, SLA language, and how you test for our specific traffic.
[03:43] Priya Nair: cost delta will be influenced by reserved baseline size and burst frequency. we'll send a matrix showing per-token cost for hosted, per-hour reserved GPU for dedicated, and an estimate for private licensing + ops. SLA terms differ — dedicated has an uptime SLA and latency SLOs with remedies; private is negotiated.
[04:02] Tom Rivers: on testing—can you run a benchmark with our prompts and traffic? we want p95 numbers for streaming per-token and overall tail latency at different concurrency levels: 100, 500, 1200.
[04:12] Marcus Lee: yes — we propose a two-stage bench: (1) a 24–48 hour sustained run at steady-state (60–120 conc) to measure steady p95 and cost; (2) a burst-profile run with ramp-up to 1200 concurrents for short windows to evaluate autoscaling and fallback behavior. we'll provide a harness using k6 + a small runner to mimic streaming token arrival.
[04:36] Aisha Khan: what about data handling during bench? can we keep sample data off Redwood logs?
[04:41] Priya Nair: yes — we support private test projects with logs disabled and can purge artifacts after the run. we also support on-prem connectors if you need no outbound payload.
[04:51] Sofia Delgado: sounds reasonable. another question — routing: if dedicated is saturated during a surge, will requests route to hosted or a smaller model? we don't want silent degradation that changes semantics.
[05:02] Marcus Lee: routing policies are explicit. you can configure automatic fallback to a compatible model variant with a clear response header indicating fallback. Also have region-based fallback. We do not silently switch model types without warning; any fallback will be logged and optionally alerted.
[05:22] Tom Rivers: good. about metrics — we need token-level cost breakdown, per-route p95, and cold-start counts. your console supports these?
[05:30] Priya Nair: yep — Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route model breakdowns, and traces for cold starts. we can export to your prometheus or datadog.
[05:39] Sofia Delgado: for streaming per-token latency, you mentioned 20–40ms p95 — is that realistic at 500 concurrent streams?
[05:46] Marcus Lee: depends on batching and HW. at 500 conc with continuous batching we often see per-token p95 around 30–45ms on dense GPUs with optimized kernels. If you have many short-turn dialogues we may need to tune batch windowing to avoid increasing latency.
[06:02] Tom Rivers: can you run a test using our network emulation (we'll add 60–200ms mobile latencies) to see end-to-end?
[06:08] Marcus Lee: yes. include the latency shim in the runner; we will report both network+inference and inference-only numbers.
[06:17] Aisha Khan: security nit — do you support SAML SSO + RBAC for our teams and per-route keying?
[06:23] Priya Nair: yes, SAML and SCIM provisioning plus fine-grained RBAC. per-route or per-model keying is available on enterprise plans.
[06:30] Sofia Delgado: another technical thing — we depend on KV cache for multi-turn sessions. how do you handle KV cache across autoscaled workers?
[06:38] Marcus Lee: we maintain session affinity so the KV cache can be kept warm; for scale-outs we propagate a compacted KV snapshot to new workers. there is a tradeoff: snapshot propagation adds some latency if done synchronously, we prefer async warm-up with request routing that favors existing warm nodes for user-facing interactions.
[06:59] Tom Rivers: what about quantized model accuracy regression? if you route to int8 variant during burst, how big is the quality delta?
[07:06] Marcus Lee: quality varies by model and dataset. in our experience int8-style quantization rarely affects surface-level factuality for short responses, but for long-form or chain-of-thought tasks it can regress. we recommend a canary policy: roll quantized variant for small percent of traffic and run evals on your prompt set — Redwood Optimize can automate that.
[07:29] Sofia Delgado: what's the typical cost trade-off? like percent cheaper for int8/gpu packing?
[07:33] Marcus Lee: ballpark 20–40% cheaper per-token depending on throughput uplift and kernel efficiency.
[07:39] Priya Nair: circling back to timelines — what's your expected pilot window and stakeholders?
[07:44] Sofia Delgado: pilots are 4–6 weeks ideally. stakeholders: myself, tom, aisha, product lead (not on call), and procurement for contracting. any big blockers unlikely, but procurement will push on data residency language.
[07:58] Marcus Lee: for procurement, we can provide our enterprise T&Cs and carve-outs for private deployments; for hosted we have standard DPA + SOC2.
[08:07] Tom Rivers: small nit on observability — can we tag requests with customer ids and propagate them through logs for debugging?
[08:12] Priya Nair: yes — request metadata tags are supported and appear in console traces.
[08:17] Sofia Delgado: on the benchmark inputs — we'll provide a mix: 60% short queries (40–80 tokens), 30% medium (100–200 tokens), 10% long summaries (~400 tokens). streaming prevalence about 70% of sessions.
[08:34] Marcus Lee: good — that distribution will help tune batch windows. for streaming-heavy workloads we often use smaller batch windows and keep a warm pool so p95 remains low.
[08:43] Tom Rivers: can you simulate sessions that maintain KV caches across sentences to mimic our real flows?
[08:48] Marcus Lee: yes — session pinning in the harness will replicate multi-turn KV behavior. we'll measure tail latency as session length grows.
[08:56] Aisha Khan: if we go private on-prem, what's the deployment footprint and ops requirements?
[09:02] Marcus Lee: depends on model family. a 7B quantized cluster for your expected steady state might be a handful of racked nodes; private comes with a deployment package and runbook. Redwood provides install support for the first rollouts. network topology, NFS, and KMS setup will be needed.
[09:20] Sofia Delgado: one more question — for dedicated vs private, who handles kernel tuning and infra upgrades?
[09:26] Priya Nair: for dedicated, Redwood manages runtime and kernel improvements; you just configure policies. for private, we provide the package and can offer managed support for kernel optimizations under a support contract.
[09:38] Tom Rivers: any known regressions on model variants when moving from per-VM inference to multi-GPU sharded?
[09:44] Marcus Lee: multi-GPU outputs are consistent but you might see different latency profiles and throughput characteristics; correctness-wise we test for numerical parity but certain ops might have small float differences — not generally user-visible.
[09:58] Sofia Delgado: great. procurement and cost will be big for us. please include an estimate for 6-month committed dedicated baseline with burst headroom.
[10:07] Priya Nair: will do. Marcus — bench specifics?
[10:10] Marcus Lee: we'll need Tom's sample prompts and a traffic histogram. plan: deliver harness, run with their latencysim, collect inference-only and full E2E metrics, and deliver a report with p50/p95/p99, cold-start events, fallback counts, and cost estimates. target delivery: initial results within 72 hours after the run completes.
[10:30] Tom Rivers: sounds good. can you also capture streaming token/sec throughput and per-token p95 during the burst?
[10:36] Marcus Lee: yes — streaming token/sec and per-token p95 will be in the artifact. we'll also note queuing behaviour if batch windows cause spikes.
[10:44] Aisha Khan: last sec question — are you able to sign our data processing addendum with additional clauses about on-site audits if we pick private?
[10:52] Priya Nair: yes, for private deployments we accommodate tighter audit terms; we'll loop in legal.
[10:58] Sofia Delgado: any constraints on the benchmark compute you'd require on our side?
[11:03] Marcus Lee: none for hosted/dedicated; for private we might need transient network access to pull images and model artifacts during install. if you want fully air-gapped, we can provide a downloadable bundle but that adds time.
[11:18] Priya Nair: ok let's recap — we will: 1) Marcus to run the bench (48-hour steady + burst profile) with their latency shim, 2) Priya to send pricing matrix and SOC2 + architecture doc, 3) Tom to send prompts and traffic histogram. we'll aim for the benchmark to start by 2026-07-21.
[11:36] Sofia Delgado: that timeline works for us. any other open items?
[11:40] Tom Rivers: procurement wants an initial estimate for 6 months — include both dedicated commit and private license overhead.
[11:45] Priya Nair: yes will include. Any competitor concerns?
[11:48] Sofia Delgado: we are also talking to Infralabs for private stack and Anthropic for hosted; main deciders will be cost and audit assurances.
[11:59] Marcus Lee: we will instrument the bench to compare also against a few baseline runs so you can see delta.
[12:04] Aisha Khan: thanks, this was helpful.
[12:06] Priya Nair: thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and the benchmark harness. expect email later today.
[12:11] Sofia Delgado: thanks everyone.
[12:12] (call ends)
